messages.text:
Most validation cases now line up exactly, and the password search returns the expected passwords for the bundled archives.

Two refinements are left: short `-h` uses Clap’s compact help rather than long help, and the pure-Python AES verifier is noticeably slower on four-letter brute force, so I’m tightening the easy compatibility pieces and checking whether worker settings can help without changing output semantics.

1:# zip-password-finder
2:[![Build](https://github.com/agourlay/zip-password-finder/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/agourlay/zip-password-finder/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
3:[![Crates.io](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/zip-password-finder.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/zip-password-finder)
5:`zip-password-finder` is a tool to find the password of protected zip files.
15:- Three attack modes: brute force, dictionary, and mask attack
16:- Graceful interruption with Ctrl-C, displaying the last password tested
17:- Resume brute force from a specific password with `--startingPassword`
25:Generates all passwords for a given charset and password length range. This is the default mode when no dictionary or mask is provided.
28:zip-password-finder -i archive.zip -c lud --minPasswordLen 1 --maxPasswordLen 6
49:zip-password-finder -i archive.zip --startingPassword "abc"
54:Tests passwords from a text file, one word per line.
57:zip-password-finder -i archive.zip -p wordlist.txt
62:Generates passwords matching a pattern where each position has its own charset. This is useful when you know part of the password structure (e.g. starts with uppercase, ends with digits).
65:zip-password-finder -i archive.zip --mask '?u?l?l?l?d?d'
68:The available mask tokens are:
85:Any other character in the mask is treated as a literal.
93:zip-password-finder -i archive.zip --mask '?l?l?l?d?d'
96:zip-password-finder -i archive.zip --mask 'pass?d?d?d?d'
99:zip-password-finder -i archive.zip --mask '?u?l?l?l?l?s'
102:zip-password-finder -i archive.zip -1 "aeiou" --mask '?1?1?d'
109:Using the provided binaries in https://github.com/agourlay/zip-password-finder/releases
113:Using Cargo via [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/zip-password-finder).
116:cargo install zip-password-finder
121:You can install [`zip-password-finder`](https://aur.archlinux.org/packages?O=0&K=zip-password-finder) from the AUR using an [AUR helper](https://wiki.archlinux.org/title/AUR_helpers). For example:
124:paru -S zip-password-finder
127:## Usage
130:./zip-password-finder -h
131:Find the password of protected ZIP files
133:Usage: zip-password-finder [OPTIONS] --inputFile <inputFile>
137:  -w, --workers <workers>                        number of workers
138:  -p, --passwordDictionary <passwordDictionary>  path to a password dictionary file
139:  -c, --charset <charset>                        charset to use to generate password [default: lud]
141:      --minPasswordLen <minPasswordLen>          minimum password length [default: 1]
142:      --maxPasswordLen <maxPasswordLen>          maximum password length [default: 10]
144:  -s, --startingPassword <startingPassword>      password to start from
145:  -m, --mask <mask>                              mask pattern for mask attack (e.g. '?l?l?l?d?d')
146:  -1, --customCharset1 <customCharset1>          custom charset 1 for mask attack, referenced as ?1
147:  -2, --customCharset2 <customCharset2>          custom charset 2 for mask attack, referenced as ?2
148:  -3, --customCharset3 <customCharset3>          custom charset 3 for mask attack, referenced as ?3
149:  -4, --customCharset4 <customCharset4>          custom charset 4 for mask attack, referenced as ?4
164:The number of workers defaults to the number of physical CPU cores. You can override this with `--workers`, but using more workers than physical cores typically does not help due to contention.
166:E.g. of scalability with an 8 core CPU with 16 threads as the number of workers increases:

input.fullContext:
You are in a benchmark workspace containing a Rust reference application at ./rust-reference and an official reference CLI path recorded in ./REFERENCE_BINARY.txt.

**Goal:**
Create a Python implementation that is a 1:1 functional port of the reference application for this benchmark. For the same input, the official reference CLI and your rebuilt version must produce exactly the same observable result: exit status, stdout, and stderr.

**Reference:**
- Project: zip-password-finder
- Source language: Rust
- Target language: Python
- Repository: https://github.com/agourlay/zip-password-finder.git
- Release/tag: v0.11.1
- Commit: 7c1a4c93841220fc740ed81d3b97784e450fc6a6
- Local source copy: ./rust-reference
- Official reference CLI: read ./REFERENCE_BINARY.txt
- Behavior area: single command CLI, argument validation, dictionary/bruteforce ZIP password search

**Hard constraints:**
- Do not use Docker.
- Do not search the internet.
- Do not look for, copy, adapt, vendor, install, or import an existing Python implementation, clone, wrapper, compatibility layer, or package for this application.
- Use ./rust-reference and the official reference CLI as the only functional sources of truth.
- Implement in Python.
- Do not shell out to the official reference CLI from your implementation.
- Do not install packages that already implement this application or its command suite.
- The root deliverable must include ./compile.sh.
- ./compile.sh must build or wrap your Python implementation and leave a runnable root command named ./executable. On Windows, ./executable.exe or ./executable.cmd is also accepted.
- The first entrypoint discovered by the evaluator must itself be directly runnable on the current OS/runtime; do not leave a higher-priority wrapper, placeholder, or script that requires a different interpreter than the evaluator will use.
- The harness will run ./compile.sh and then invoke your runnable executable with the same argv used for the official reference CLI.

**Equivalence requirements:**
- For every evaluated invocation, running the official reference CLI and running your rebuilt executable with the same argv, stdin, files, and environment must produce the same exit status, stdout, and stderr.
- If the official binary prints nothing, your program must print nothing.
- If the official binary writes to stderr, your program must write to stderr.

**Do not ask the user questions.** Infer from source and official CLI behavior.
